The Past Perfect, Simple Past and Past Continuous Tenses

You use the Past Perfect tense to identify and talk about an 'earlier past'.
You use the Past Continuous tense to talk about an action that was happening at a time before now.
You use the Simple Past to talk about a finished action that happened at a specific time in the past.

When you are talking about a past event, you can refer to something that happened at an earlier time to that past event by using the Past Perfect tense.

The structure of the Past Perfect is:

Subject + had + past participle

When I arrived at the party, Vanessa had already gone home.
Which event happened first? Vanessa went home.
Which event happened later? I arrived at the party.

You use the Past Perfect tense (not Simple Past) when you want to talk about how long something had continued up to a past moment.

You can use the Past Continuous to:

  • describe the background in a story written in the past tense

For example:
The children were laughing and the birds were singing in the park. A woman was looking for her phone, which she had dropped somewhere ...

  • to describe an action that was interrupted by another event or action in the Simple Past

For example:
I was reading the news the other day when I came across an article that talked about a trial by judge.

The form of the Past Continuous is:

Subject + was/were + verb-ing
Maria woke up to the false calm of the green hospital walls.
Her parents were smiling down at her.
Your father and I brought you some nice little gifts.
All the stuff in her room was exactly as she had left it before the surgery.
She had had a bad dream - that was the only explanation!
Her father was also coming over to give her a hug when he almost slipped on something on the floor.
a temporary calm a person feels that doesn't reveal their actual usual nature
Example: Maria woke up to the false calm of the green hospital walls.
These are words you use to talk about strange experiences.
to lose balance or fall because of accidentally sliding
Example: He almost slipped on something on the floor.
a person in charge of maintaining a property
Example: The custodian here could clean up that broken glass on the floor.
having a rough and unclear voice
Example: “Of course", the old man said in his soft hoarse voice.
to quickly close and open an eye to communicate something secretly
Example: The man winked and said: "Glad to see you're feeling better."
in a way that shows knowledge of private or secret information
Example: “I know you want to call my friend!”, she said knowingly.

images.text:
Maria woke up to the false calm of the green hospital walls. Her parents were smiling down at her.
"Maria, honey," her mother said softly, "good morning, dear. Your father and I brought you some nice little gifts. Does your leg hurt badly?"
Maria was so happy to see her mother. She looked down at her body and saw that it was her own. She felt her face ... Yes, it was her own face. All the stuff in her room was exactly as she had left it before the surgery. She had had a bad dream - that was the only explanation!

"Oh, Mother! Yes, my leg hurts ... It's so wonderful! I had this awful dream that I ... Well, it doesn't matter, I'm just glad to see you," Maria said, as she was given a big kiss. Her father was also coming over to give her a hug when he almost slipped on something on the floor.
"A broken glass! This should be cleaned up immediately. I could have slipped and hurt myself! Here, I'll give you a hug and find someone to clean this up.”

Maria's father gave her a quick hug and started for the door. Just as he was leaving, he bumped into the old man with the mop who had appeared at the door.
"Here's a custodian!" Maria's father said. "Could you clean up that broken glass on the floor over there?" he asked the old man. "It's really very dangerous." He had looked over at Maria.
"Of course," the old man said in his soft hoarse voice. Then, he winked. "Glad to see you're feeling better," he said knowingly.
